title: Digital Skills: Google Classroom and the Cloud
summary: The digital skills you need at secondary school: what the cloud is, using Google Classroom and Drive, collaborating safely in Docs, Slides and Sheets, staying organised and being a responsible digital citizen.
learn: What the cloud and remote storage are, their pros and cons, and the environmental cost of data centres
How to join a Google Classroom class, find assignments, turn in and unsubmit work
How to organise Google Drive with folders and sensible file names, and how the operating system manages local files
How to use Docs, Slides and Sheets with autosave and version history
How to share with the right permission, and the difference between synchronous and asynchronous collaboration
How to upload and convert files, stay organised and meet deadlines
How to communicate for your audience, avoid plagiarism, protect personal data (UK GDPR) and fix common problems
intro: At secondary school most of your work lives in the cloud. This topic builds on your MySchool login and school email: you will learn how Google Classroom and Google Drive work, how to hand in work properly, how to collaborate on shared documents, and how to stay organised, safe and responsible online. It links to the NI TransformED Digital Technology framework: collaboration tools (C6), communicating for an audience (C5), how the operating system manages files and remote storage (S9), personal data and GDPR (E4) and the environmental cost of the cloud (E6).

pages.spec: Explain what the cloud is and compare saving work in cloud storage with saving it on a device
pages.summary: The cloud means using storage and software on someone else's computers (servers in data centres) over the internet. Cloud storage lets you reach your work from any device, but you need an internet connection and a secure password.

diagram.title: Saving on a device vs saving in the cloud
diagram.caption: Two places your work can be saved. Neither is perfect.

states.label: Saved on a device (local storage)
points: Kept on the device's own drive or a USB stick
Only on that one device, unless you copy it
Lost if the device or stick is lost, broken or stolen

states.label: Saved in the cloud
points: Kept on servers in a data centre, reached over the internet
Open it from any device: school, home or phone
Needs an internet connection (unless set up for offline use)
Protected only as well as your password

blocks.text: At primary school you may have saved work on the computer in front of you, or on a USB stick. At secondary school most of your work will be saved **in the cloud**. So what is the cloud, and why does everyone talk about it as if it were floating above our heads?
What is the cloud?

**[[The cloud|Cloud]]** is a nickname for computers, storage and software that you use **over the internet** instead of on your own device. Your files are not really in the sky: they are stored on powerful computers called **servers**, in huge buildings called **[[data centres|Data centre]]**. Companies such as Google, Microsoft and Apple run data centres all over the world.

**[[Cloud storage]]** means saving your files on those servers. It is a type of **[[remote storage|Remote storage]]**: storage that is somewhere else, not inside the device in front of you. **[[Local storage]]** means saving them on the device you are using: its hard drive or SSD, or a USB stick plugged into it.
A good way to remember it: *the cloud is just someone else's computer*. You are borrowing space on their servers, and you reach it through the internet.
Cloud services you might already use

head: Service
What it does in the cloud
rows: Stores your files and folders online
Software that runs in your web browser, so nothing needs to be installed
Your teachers post work and you hand it in online
Online file storage and your C2k school email
The songs or films stay on the company's servers and are sent to you as you watch or listen
blocks.caption: Everyday cloud services

blocks.text: When software itself runs over the internet, like Google Docs in a web browser, this is called **[[cloud computing]]**. You do not install Google Docs on the school computer: it runs on Google's servers and your browser shows you the result.
Cloud storage vs local storage

head: Cloud storage
Local storage
rows: On servers in a data centre
On the device or a USB stick
Can I reach it from home?
Yes, from any device with the internet
Only if I bring the device or stick with me
Usually cannot open or save it
Work is safe: just sign in on another device
Work may be lost unless there is a backup
Several people can edit the same file at once
You have to send copies back and forth

blocks.text: Advantages of cloud storage

items: **Access anywhere**: start a homework in the ICT room in Enniskillen and finish it at home, at your gran's or on a phone.
**[[Autosave]]**: Google Docs, Sheets and Slides save every change automatically, so a power cut does not wipe out your work.
**Nothing to carry or lose**: no USB stick to leave in your blazer pocket and put through the wash.
**Collaboration**: several pupils can work on the same document at the same time.
**Backed up by the provider**: data centres keep extra copies of data, so a single broken server does not lose your file.
**Saves space** on your own device.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of cloud storage

items: **Needs an internet connection**: if the Wi-Fi is down, you may not be able to open your work.
**Security depends on your password**: if someone learns it, they can see and change all your files from anywhere in the world.
**Privacy**: your files are kept by another company, so you have to trust how it looks after them.
**Large files can be slow** to upload or download on a slow connection.
**Outages**: very occasionally a cloud service goes down and nobody can reach their files for a while.

blocks.text: The hidden cost: energy and water

The cloud may feel weightless, but it is very real. Data centres are packed with thousands of servers that run **24 hours a day**. They use a lot of **electricity**, both to run the servers and to keep them cool, and many use **water** for cooling too. Where that electricity comes from fossil fuels, it adds to **carbon emissions**. This is called the **[[environmental cost|Environmental cost]]** of cloud services, and AI tools that run in data centres add to it.

Every file you keep in the cloud is stored, and backed up, on servers that use energy. Good digital habits, like deleting files you will never need again and not uploading ten copies of the same video, help a little. You will see more on page 4.

Cloud storage is **not** magic protection. If **you** delete a file or type over your best paragraph, the cloud saves that mistake too. That is why version history (page 5) and the Bin (page 4) are so useful.

blocks.title: Worked example: cloud or USB stick?
blocks.context: Erin is making a Slides presentation with two friends for a history project. She will work on it in school, at home in Belleek and on the bus on her phone.
steps: She needs to reach it from **three different places**: cloud storage wins.
Two friends need to edit the **same** presentation: cloud storage allows real-time collaboration.
A USB stick could be lost on the bus and only one person can have it at a time.
One disadvantage to plan for: on the bus there may be no signal, so she should not leave everything to the last minute.
blocks.answer: Cloud storage (Google Drive / Slides) is the better choice, because she needs access from many devices and must collaborate.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The cloud = storage and software on servers in data centres, used over the internet.
Cloud storage saves files online; local storage saves them on the device or a USB stick.
Advantages: access anywhere, autosave, collaboration, nothing to lose, provider keeps backups.
Disadvantages: needs the internet, depends on a strong password, privacy, slow with large files.
Data centres use lots of electricity and water: the cloud has an environmental cost.
The cloud also saves your mistakes, so you still need to be careful.

check.q: What is 'the cloud' really?
o: Storage space inside the satellites that orbit the Earth
The hard drive inside the school computer you are using
Servers in data centres that you use over the internet
A special USB stick that connects to the internet
check.why: Cloud files are stored on servers in data centres and reached over the internet.

check.q: Which is an advantage of cloud storage over a USB stick?

It works even when there is no internet connection at all
Nobody else could ever see your files, even with your password
Your files can never be deleted, even by mistake
check.why: Access from any internet-connected device is the main advantage.

check.q: Which is a disadvantage of cloud storage?
o: You have to carry the storage device with you everywhere
Only one person can ever open a file at a time
You usually need an internet connection to reach your files
Files cannot be shared with your teacher
check.why: Without an internet connection you usually cannot open or save cloud files.

check.q: Saving a file on the laptop's own SSD is an example of:
check.why: Storage on the device itself is local storage.

check.q: Why do cloud services have an environmental cost?
o: Cloud files are printed out and stored on paper as a backup
Every file you save makes your own laptop use more battery all week
Data centres can only be built by cutting down forests
Data centres use lots of electricity and water to run and cool servers
check.why: Servers run all day and need cooling, using energy and often water.

practice.q: What is meant by **cloud storage**?
practice.a: Saving files on servers / remote computers owned by another company (1), which are accessed over the internet (1).

practice.q: Give **two** advantages and **one** disadvantage of saving your schoolwork in the cloud rather than on a USB stick.
practice.a: Advantages (any two): access from any device / anywhere with internet (1); cannot lose or break it like a USB stick (1); autosave (1); easy to collaborate/share (1); provider keeps backups (1). Disadvantage (any one): needs an internet connection / someone with your password can get in / privacy concerns / large files slow to upload (1).

practice.q: Erin says: "My work is in the cloud, so it can never be lost." Explain why she is not completely right.
practice.a: If she deletes or overwrites it herself, the cloud saves that change too (1); someone who gets her password could delete it / the service could be unavailable / no internet (1).

pages.spec: Sign in to Google Classroom with your school account, join a class with a class code and use the Stream, Classwork and People pages
pages.summary: Sign in with your C2k school Google account, join each class with the code your teacher gives you, then use the Stream for announcements, Classwork for assignments and materials, and People to see who is in the class.

diagram.title: Inside a Google Classroom class
diagram.caption: Click each part of a class to see what it is for. The exact layout changes from time to time, but these parts are always there.

rows.label: Class name and banner
rows.detail: Tells you which class you are in, e.g. 8B ICT. Check this before you post anything!

rows.label: Your profile picture
rows.detail: Top right. Click it to see which account you are signed in with, or to switch account.

rows.label: Stream
rows.detail: The class noticeboard: announcements from your teacher and a post for each new piece of work.

rows.label: Classwork
rows.detail: Every assignment, question and material, sorted into topics. The best place to find work.

rows.label: People
rows.detail: The teachers and classmates in this class.

blocks.text: **[[Google Classroom]]** is a website (and app) where your teachers post work, notes and announcements, and where you hand in your work. You met it briefly when you started ICT. On this page you will learn to find your way around it properly.
Signing in with the right account

In Northern Irish schools your Google account comes from **C2k**, the same system as your MySchool login. Your school Google account is your **C2k username followed by @c2ken.net**, and the password is your normal school password.

items: In school, you can reach Google Classroom through **MySchool**, or by signing in to Google in the web browser.
At home, go to the Google Classroom website (or install the Classroom app) and sign in with **yourusername@c2ken.net** and your school password.
Look at the **profile picture** in the top right: it shows which account is signed in.

blocks.text: If you are signed in with a **personal** Gmail account (or a brother's or sister's account), your classes will not appear and you will not be able to join with the code. This is the number one problem pupils have. Always check which account you are using.
Joining a class
Each class has a **[[class code]]**: a short code of **6 to 8 letters and numbers**, with no spaces. Your teacher will put it on the board, give it to you on a slip, or invite you directly.

items: Open Google Classroom.
Click the **+** (or **Join class**).
Type the class code **exactly**, including capital letters.
Click **Join**.

blocks.text: You only need the class code once. After you have joined, the class appears as a card on your Classroom home page on every device you sign in to.
Sometimes a teacher adds you to a class instead. You will then see an invitation in Classroom or in your email, and you just click **Join**.
The pages in a class

head: Page
What you find there
When to use it
rows: Announcements from your teacher, and a short post whenever new work is set
Check it at the start of each lesson for news and reminders
All the **[[assignments|Assignment]]**, questions and materials, grouped into **topics**
To find a piece of work, notes or a worksheet
The names of your teachers and classmates
To check who is in the class
blocks.caption: The main pages of a Google Classroom class

blocks.text: On the Classwork page, teachers can post three main kinds of thing: an **assignment** (work you hand in), a **question** (a short answer or a multiple-choice question) and **material** (notes, links or videos to read or watch, with nothing to hand in).

blocks.title: Worked example: where would you look?
blocks.context: Callum has just joined 8C ICT. Where should he look for each of these?
steps: (a) A message from Mr Butler saying "Room change: we are in ICT2 today": the **Stream**.
(b) Last week's worksheet on file extensions, which he missed: **Classwork**, under the right topic.
(c) Whether his friend Oisín is in the same class: **People**.
blocks.answer: Stream for news, Classwork for work and notes, People for who is in the class.

blocks.text: Do not type the class code with spaces or change capital letters to small ones. If it still does not work, check your account first, then tell your teacher.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Sign in with your school account: username@c2ken.net and your school password.
Join a class once with its 6 to 8 character class code.
Stream = announcements and news. Classwork = assignments, questions and materials by topic. People = who is in the class.
Your profile picture (top right) shows which account you are using.

check.q: Which page of a class lists all the assignments and materials, sorted into topics?
check.why: Classwork holds all the work, grouped by topic.

check.q: Niamh types the class code correctly but Classroom says it cannot find the class. What is the most likely reason?
o: Class codes only work on school computers
She is signed in with her personal Gmail account
She needs to type the code in lower-case letters
The class is already full of pupils
check.why: Using the wrong account is the most common reason a correct code fails.

check.q: How long is a Google Classroom class code?
check.why: Class codes are 6 to 8 letters and numbers with no spaces.

check.q: Where would you expect to see your teacher's announcement that the lesson has moved room?
check.why: Announcements appear on the Stream.

check.q: What is a pupil's C2k Google account address made of?
o: Their date of birth followed by @school.com
check.why: School Google accounts in NI are username@c2ken.net.

practice.q: Describe how to join a Google Classroom class using a class code.
practice.a: Sign in with your school (@c2ken.net) account (1); click + / Join class (1); enter the code exactly as given and click Join (1).

practice.q: State what you would find on the **Stream** and on the **Classwork** page.
practice.a: Stream: announcements / news from the teacher / posts about new work (1). Classwork: the assignments, questions and materials, organised into topics (1).

practice.q: Give **one** reason why a pupil might not be able to see their classes when they sign in at home.
practice.a: Signed in with the wrong (personal/family) Google account / not signed in with @c2ken.net (1).

pages.spec: Find, open and hand in an assignment, unsubmit work if needed, and use private and class comments correctly
pages.summary: Open an assignment from Classwork or your To-do list, read the instructions and due date, do the work, attach anything needed and click Turn in. Unsubmit if you need to change it. Private comments go only to your teacher; class comments are seen by everyone.

diagram.title: The life of an assignment
diagram.caption: Click each stage. If you unsubmit, the work goes back to you to edit.

nodes.label: Assigned
nodes.detail: Your teacher sets the work. It appears on the Stream, on Classwork and in your To-do list.

nodes.label: Open and read
nodes.detail: Read the instructions, the due date and any attached files. A file marked 'Make a copy for each student' gives you your own copy.

nodes.label: Do the work
nodes.detail: Work in your copy, or create or upload a file with Add or create. It saves automatically.

nodes.label: Turn in
nodes.detail: Click Turn in (or Mark as done if there is nothing to attach). Your teacher can now mark it.

nodes.label: Unsubmit?
nodes.detail: Spotted a mistake before the teacher marks it? Click Unsubmit, fix it, and Turn in again.

nodes.label: Returned
nodes.detail: Your teacher marks the work and returns it, often with comments or a mark.

blocks.text: An **[[assignment]]** is a piece of work your teacher sets in Google Classroom for you to complete and hand in. Handing work in online is called **[[turning in|Turn in]]** the work.
Finding your assignments

items: On the **Classwork** page of the class, under the right topic.
On the **Stream**, where a post appears whenever new work is set.
In your **To-do** list, which collects work from *all* your classes (more on page 9).
From an email or notification telling you about new work.

blocks.text: Inside an assignment

head: Part
What it tells you
rows: What you have to do. Read them all before you start!
The date (and sometimes time) the work must be turned in by. Some work has no due date.
How many marks it is out of, if your teacher has set this.
Worksheets or templates from your teacher. If it says you get your **own copy**, your name is added to the file name and only you and your teacher can edit it.
Shows the status (Assigned, Missing, Turned in) and the **Turn in** button. **Add or create** lets you attach a Google Drive file, a link or an uploaded file, or create a new Doc, Slides or Sheet.
Class comments and private comments (see below).
blocks.caption: The parts of an assignment

blocks.text: Turning in your work

items: Open the assignment.
Open your copy of the file (or click **Add or create** to attach your work).
Finish the work. Google files save automatically.
Read the instructions once more: have you done everything?
Click **Turn in**, then confirm.

blocks.text: If there is nothing to attach (for example, the task was to read some notes), the button says **Mark as done** instead.

**Attaching a file is not the same as turning it in!** Lots of pupils attach their work, close the page and think they are finished. Until you click **Turn in**, your teacher sees the work as not handed in, and after the due date it shows as **Missing**.
Unsubmitting

Spotted a mistake after you turned in? Click **[[Unsubmit]]**. The work goes back to you so you can edit it, but you **must click Turn in again** afterwards. If the due date has passed, it will then show as turned in **late**.
When you turn in a Google file, you usually cannot edit it any more until you unsubmit or your teacher returns it. That is normal, not a fault.
Private comments and class comments

head: Private comment
Class comment
rows: Inside the assignment, in the **Private comments** box
Under the post on the Stream or in the assignment
"I was absent, can I have until Friday?" or a question about your own work
"Is the homework the worksheet or the quiz?": a question that helps everyone
Personal things, or anything you would not say in front of the whole class

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Grace do?
blocks.context: Grace's assignment was due on Tuesday. On Monday night she turned it in, then realised she had forgotten her conclusion. She also wants to tell Mr Butler she was off sick last week.
steps: Click **Unsubmit** on the assignment.
Add the conclusion to her document.
Click **Turn in** again before Tuesday's due date, so it is not late.
Use a **private comment** to tell Mr Butler she was off sick, because that is personal and only he needs to know.
blocks.answer: Unsubmit, fix, Turn in again before the deadline, and use a private comment for the personal message.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Assignments are on Classwork, the Stream and your To-do list.
Read the instructions and due date first.
Attaching is not enough: you must click Turn in (or Mark as done).
Unsubmit to make changes, then Turn in again.
Private comments: you and the teacher only. Class comments: everyone.

check.q: Ruairí attached his finished document to the assignment and closed the page. What has he forgotten?
check.why: Attaching is not handing in; he must click Turn in.

check.q: Who can read a private comment on an assignment?
check.why: Private comments are between you and the teacher.

check.q: What does Unsubmit do?
o: Takes the work back so you can change it
Sends the work to the whole class
Moves the due date back a week
check.why: Unsubmit returns the work to you to edit; you must turn it in again.

check.q: An assignment asks you to read some notes, with nothing to attach. Which button will you see?
check.why: With nothing attached, the button says Mark as done.

practice.q: Describe the steps to hand in an assignment in Google Classroom.
practice.a: Open the assignment from Classwork/Stream/To-do (1); open your copy or attach the file using Add or create (1); click Turn in and confirm (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a private comment and a class comment.
practice.a: A private comment can only be seen by you and the teacher (1); a class comment can be seen by everyone in the class (1).

practice.q: Oisín turned in his work, then unsubmitted it to fix a spelling mistake. Explain what he must remember to do next.
practice.a: Click Turn in again (1), otherwise the work counts as not handed in / missing after the due date (1).

pages.spec: Use Google Drive to create folders, give files sensible names and organise your work
pages.summary: Google Drive is your cloud filing cabinet. Use New to create folders, give every file a clear name that says what it is, and keep work in a simple folder structure so you can always find it. Deleted files go to the Bin first.

diagram.title: Good file name or bad file name?
diagram.caption: Decide whether each name is good, then click to check.
head: File name
Good or bad?
Why
rows: Says nothing about what is inside
Random letters: you will never find it
Which one is actually the final version?
Rename copies so they say what they are

blocks.text: **[[Google Drive]]** is Google's cloud storage. Every file you make in Google Docs, Sheets or Slides is saved in your Drive, and you can also upload other files to it. Think of it as a filing cabinet you can open from any device.
The main areas of Drive

head: Area
What it holds
rows: Files and folders you own or have added. Your main workspace.
Files other people have shared with you, such as a group project.
Files you opened or changed recently: a quick way back to today's work.
Files you have marked with a star because you use them a lot.
Files you have deleted. They stay here for **30 days** and can be restored, then they are deleted for good.
blocks.caption: Google Drive

blocks.text: Google Classroom automatically makes a **Classroom** folder in your Drive, with a folder for each class. Copies of assignment files you work on are kept there. You do not need to move them.
Creating a folder

items: In Google Drive, click **New**.
Choose **New folder**.
Type a sensible name, e.g. *ICT*.
Click **Create**. Double-click the folder to open it, and make folders inside it in the same way.

blocks.text: You can drag files into folders, or right-click a file and choose to move or organise it. You learned about folders, subfolders and the root folder in your first ICT topic; Drive works in exactly the same way.
Sensible file names
A good **file name** tells you what is inside **without opening it**. A useful pattern is **subject + topic + what it is**, for example *ICT Cloud Storage Notes* or *Geography Lough Erne Fieldwork*.

items: Never leave a file called **Untitled document**: click the title at the top left of a Google file to rename it straight away.
Rename files that start with **Copy of**.
Keep names fairly short, but clear.
If you need several versions, number them clearly (Draft 1, Draft 2), though in Google files version history usually does this job for you.

blocks.title: Worked example: organise Jack's Drive
blocks.context: Jack's My Drive has 23 files all loose together, including *Untitled document*, *Untitled document (1)*, *maths thing* and *Copy of ICT worksheet*.
steps: Create one folder per subject: **ICT**, **Maths**, **English**, **History**...
Open each file, see what it is, and rename it: *Untitled document* becomes *English Persuasive Letter*.
Rename *Copy of ICT worksheet* to *ICT File Extensions Worksheet*.
Drag each file into its subject folder. Inside ICT, add topic folders if there are lots of files.
Delete files that are truly empty; they go to the Bin, so nothing is lost by mistake for 30 days.
blocks.answer: A folder for each subject and clear names mean Jack can find any piece of work in seconds.

blocks.text: Use the **search box** at the top of Drive. Good file names make searching work: searching *photosynthesis* finds *Science Photosynthesis Notes*, but not *Untitled document*.
Deleting a folder deletes **everything inside it**. Check before you delete, and remember the Bin empties itself after 30 days.
Who manages files on your own device?

On a laptop or school PC, files saved **locally** are looked after by the **[[operating system]]** (such as Windows, macOS or ChromeOS). The operating system keeps track of where every file is stored on the drive, lets you create, rename, move and delete files and folders (for example in File Explorer on Windows), and controls **who** is allowed to open them. Google Drive does the same jobs for your **remote** files, but on Google's servers instead of your device.
Sustainable digital habits

Because every stored file uses energy in a data centre (page 1), a tidy Drive is a greener Drive. **[[Sustainable digital habits|Sustainable digital habit]]** are small, everyday choices that cut the energy and storage your digital life uses:

items: Delete old files, duplicate copies and blurry photos you will never use.
Share a **link** to one file instead of attaching copies to lots of emails.
Do not upload the same large video several times.
Empty the Bin when you are sure you do not need what is in it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Google Drive is cloud storage for all your Google files and uploads.
My Drive, Shared with me, Recent, Starred and Bin.
New > New folder to create folders; drag files in to organise them.
Good file names say subject + topic + what it is. No 'Untitled document'!
Deleted files stay in the Bin for 30 days.
On your own device the operating system manages files; deleting files you do not need is a sustainable habit.

check.q: Which is the best file name for your ICT homework on cloud storage?
check.why: It says the subject, the topic and what it is.

check.q: Where in Google Drive would you find a group project file that a friend shared with you?
check.why: Files shared by other people appear in Shared with me.

check.q: How long do deleted files usually stay in the Bin in Google Drive?
check.why: Files stay in the Bin for 30 days before being permanently deleted.

check.q: How do you start creating a new folder in Google Drive?
o: Open the Bin and click Restore
check.why: New > New folder creates a folder.

check.q: On a Windows laptop, what keeps track of where locally saved files are stored?
check.why: The operating system manages files on the device.

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why you should give files sensible names.
practice.a: Any two: you can tell what is in a file without opening it (1); easier to find/search for later (1); avoids opening/handing in the wrong file (1); others you share with know what it is (1).

practice.q: Suggest a sensible folder structure in Google Drive for a Year 8 pupil's schoolwork.
practice.a: A main folder (e.g. Year 8) / folders for each subject (1); topic subfolders inside each subject (1).

practice.q: Explain what happens to a file when you delete it in Google Drive.
practice.a: It moves to the Bin (1) where it can be restored for 30 days before it is permanently deleted (1).

pages.spec: Use Google Docs, Slides and Sheets for the right tasks, and explain autosave and version history
pages.summary: Docs is for writing, Slides for presentations and Sheets for numbers and tables. They run in the browser, save automatically to Drive, and keep a version history so you can see and restore earlier versions of your work.

diagram.title: Which Google app?
diagram.caption: Match each app to the job it does best.
pairs: Google Docs
Writing a letter or a story
Google Slides
A presentation for the class
Google Sheets
Calculating the cost of a school trip
Google Forms
A survey of your classmates
Google Drive
Storing and organising all your files
Version history
Getting back yesterday's paragraph

blocks.text: Google's office apps run in your **web browser**, so you can use them on any computer, Chromebook, tablet or phone without installing anything. They are like the Microsoft Word, PowerPoint and Excel programs you may already know.

head: App
Like...
Use it for
rows: Word processing: letters, essays, reports, stories
Presentations with slides, images and speaker notes
Spreadsheets: tables of numbers, formulas, charts
blocks.caption: Google's main apps

blocks.text: Creating a new file

items: In Google Drive: click **New**, then choose Google Docs, Google Sheets or Google Slides.
In a Classroom assignment: click **Add or create** and choose the type of file. It is attached to that assignment for you.
Then **rename it** straight away by clicking *Untitled* at the top left.

blocks.text: Autosave

There is no Save button. **[[Autosave]]** means every change is saved to Google Drive automatically, a moment after you make it. Near the file name you will briefly see a message such as *Saving...* and then a cloud icon showing it has been saved to Drive.

Autosave only works while you are **online**. If the Wi-Fi drops, Google may show that it is offline or cannot save. Do not close the tab until it says your changes are saved, or you could lose the last few minutes of work.
Version history
Because Google saves as you go, it also keeps a record of **earlier versions** of the file. This is called **[[version history]]**. It shows who changed what, and when.

items: Open the file.
Click **File**, then **Version history**, then **See version history**.
Click a date and time on the right to see the file as it was then. Changes made by different people are shown in different colours.
To go back to it, click **Restore this version**.

blocks.title: Worked example: the disappearing paragraph
blocks.context: On Wednesday night Callum accidentally selected half of his English essay and typed over it. Autosave saved the mistake straight away, and Undo did not go back far enough.
steps: Open the essay and choose **File > Version history > See version history**.
Look at the list of times on the right and click the version from **Wednesday afternoon**, before the mistake.
Check that the missing paragraphs are there.
Click **Restore this version**.
blocks.answer: Version history brings the whole essay back. Nothing he did on Wednesday afternoon is lost.

blocks.text: Version history also shows your teacher **who wrote what** in a shared document, so it is easy to see if someone in a group did not do their share, or copied and pasted a lot of text in one go.
Handy basics in all three apps

items: **Ctrl + Z** undoes, **Ctrl + Y** redoes.
**Ctrl + C** copies, **Ctrl + V** pastes, **Ctrl + B** makes text bold.
**Tools > Spelling and grammar** checks your spelling (set the language to English (UK) if it keeps changing *colour* to *color*).
**Insert** adds images, tables, charts and links.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Docs = writing, Slides = presentations, Sheets = numbers and tables, Forms = surveys.
They run in the browser and save automatically to Drive (autosave).
Rename new files straight away.
File > Version history > See version history lets you see and restore earlier versions.
Autosave needs an internet connection.

check.q: Which Google app is best for working out the total cost of a class trip?
check.why: Sheets is a spreadsheet for numbers and calculations.

check.q: What does autosave mean in Google Docs?
o: Changes are saved to Drive automatically as you work
You must click Save every five minutes
The file is saved to a USB stick when you close it
Your teacher saves a copy of the file each night
check.why: Google files save each change automatically while you are online.

check.q: Callum typed over half his essay and it autosaved. What should he use to get the old text back?
check.why: Version history lets him restore an earlier version.

check.q: Where is version history found in Google Docs?
o: File > Version history > See version history
check.why: It is under the File menu.

check.q: Which of these is TRUE about autosave?
o: It means you can never lose any work at all
It saves files to the computer's desktop
It only works in Google Slides
It needs an internet connection to save to Drive
check.why: Autosave saves to Drive, so it needs a connection.

practice.q: Name the most suitable Google app for each task: (a) a poster-style presentation for a class talk, (b) a letter to a local councillor, (c) a table of rugby scores with an average.
practice.a: (a) Google Slides (1); (b) Google Docs (1); (c) Google Sheets (1).

practice.q: Explain what version history is and give **one** situation where it would be useful.
practice.a: A record of earlier versions of a file / who changed what and when (1); e.g. restoring work that was deleted or overwritten by mistake / seeing who did what in a group project (1).

practice.q: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of autosave.
practice.a: Advantage: you do not lose work if you forget to save / the computer crashes (1). Disadvantage: it also saves mistakes immediately / needs an internet connection (1).

pages.spec: Share a file with the right permission (viewer, commenter or editor) and use comments and suggesting mode
pages.summary: The Share button lets you choose who can open a file and what they can do: viewers can only look, commenters can add comments and suggestions, editors can change everything. Suggesting mode and comments let people improve work without overwriting it.

diagram.title: Which permission?
diagram.caption: Pick the permission you would give, then click to check.
head: Situation
Best permission
rows: Your group of three is writing one Slides presentation together
Your friend will check your story and suggest improvements
You want your granny to see your finished poster
The class needs to read a timetable but must not change it
Your teacher wants to leave feedback but not change your words

blocks.text: One of the best things about Google Drive is that you can **share** a file, so other people can see it or work on it with you. The person who created the file is its **owner**, and the owner decides who gets in and what they can do.
The three permissions

head: Permission
They can...
They cannot...
rows: Change anything, and (usually) share it with others
Nothing is off-limits, so trust them!
blocks.caption: Sharing permissions

blocks.text: Together these are called **[[sharing permissions|Sharing permission]]**. Give people the **lowest permission they need**: if someone only needs to read your work, make them a viewer.
How to share a file

items: Open the file (or right-click it in Drive).
Click **Share**.
Type the person's school email address (e.g. their username@c2ken.net).
Choose **Viewer**, **Commenter** or **Editor** from the drop-down.
Click **Send** (or **Share**).

blocks.text: Be careful with **"Anyone with the link"**. It means anybody who gets the link, even a stranger, can open the file. In school, share with named people instead. C2k may also stop you sharing outside the school system.
Comments

A **comment** is a note attached to part of a document, like a sticky note in the margin. Select some text, then click the comment button (or **Insert > Comment**), type your note and click **Comment**. Others can reply, and when the problem is fixed someone clicks **Resolve** to tidy it away.
Suggesting mode

In **[[suggesting mode]]** your changes are not made straight away. Instead they appear in **colour** as *suggestions*, and the owner decides whether to **accept** (tick) or **reject** (cross) each one. Switch modes using the pencil/mode button near the top right: **Editing**, **Suggesting** or **Viewing**.

head: Editing mode
Suggesting mode
rows: Your change is shown in colour as a suggestion
The owner accepts or rejects it
Your own work, or agreed group work

blocks.title: Worked example: peer review
blocks.context: Niamh asks Jack to check her English story before she hands it in. She does not want him to change her words without her knowing.
steps: Niamh clicks **Share** and adds Jack as a **Commenter**.
Jack spots *their* where it should be *there*. Because he is a commenter, his change appears as a **suggestion**.
He selects a weak ending and adds a **comment**: *Maybe say how the dog got home?*
Niamh accepts the spelling suggestion, rewrites the ending, then **resolves** the comment.
blocks.answer: Commenter permission plus suggestions and comments lets Jack help without taking over Niamh's work.

blocks.text: You can type **@** and a classmate's name in a comment to tag them. They get an email telling them to look at it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Share button: choose people and a permission.
Viewer = read only. Commenter = comments and suggestions. Editor = change anything.
Give the lowest permission people need; avoid 'Anyone with the link'.
Comments are notes in the margin; resolve them when done.
Suggesting mode shows changes in colour for the owner to accept or reject.

check.q: Which permission lets someone add comments but not change your text directly?
check.why: Commenters can comment and suggest, but not edit directly.

check.q: Your group is writing one Slides presentation together. What permission should each member have?
check.why: Everyone needs to change the slides, so they need editor access.

check.q: In suggesting mode, what happens when you type?
o: Your change shows in colour for the owner to accept or reject
The text changes for good and the owner cannot undo it
Your typing is sent as an email to the owner
Nothing happens until you click Save
check.why: Suggestions wait for the owner to accept or reject them.

check.q: Why is 'Anyone with the link' risky?
o: It deletes the file after one day
It makes everyone an owner of the file
Anyone who gets the link, even a stranger, can open the file
It stops your teacher from seeing the file
check.why: The link can be passed on to anyone.

practice.q: Describe the difference between a **viewer** and an **editor** of a shared document.
practice.a: A viewer can only open/read the document (1); an editor can change the content (and usually share it) (1).

practice.q: Explain why a pupil might use **suggesting mode** when checking a friend's work.
practice.a: Changes appear as suggestions rather than being made directly (1), so the owner keeps control and can accept or reject each one (1).

practice.q: Erin wants her teacher to give feedback on her essay without changing it. Which permission should she give and why?
practice.a: Commenter (1), because the teacher can add comments/suggestions but cannot change the text directly (1).

pages.spec: Compare synchronous and asynchronous collaboration tools and work on a shared document responsibly
pages.summary: Synchronous collaboration happens in real time, like live co-editing or a video call. Asynchronous collaboration happens at different times, using shared folders, comments and online workspaces. Good collaborators split the work, stay in their own section and never delete other people's work.

diagram.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous collaboration
diagram.caption: Two ways of working together online. Most projects use both.

states.label: Synchronous (at the same time)
points: Live co-editing: everyone in one Doc at once
Video calls, e.g. Google Meet or Microsoft Teams
Everyone must be free and online together

states.label: Asynchronous (at different times)
points: Comments and replies in a document
Online workspaces such as a Classroom stream
Work when it suits you, but replies can be slow

blocks.text: **Collaboration** means working together with other people to make something. Online platforms like Google Workspace make it easy for a group to collaborate even when they are not in the same room. There are two kinds of online collaboration, and the words for them are worth learning.
Synchronous collaboration
**[[Synchronous collaboration]]** means working together **at the same time**, in real time. *Syn* means together and *chronos* means time.

items: **Live co-editing**: three pupils open the same Google Doc at once. Each person's cursor appears in a different colour with their name, and you can watch the others typing.
**Video calls** such as Google Meet or Microsoft Teams: talking and sharing a screen face to face.
**Live chat** while you all work on the same file.

blocks.text: Asynchronous collaboration
**[[Asynchronous collaboration]]** means working together **at different times**. One person adds something, and the others pick it up later when it suits them.

items: **Shared folders** in Google Drive, where everyone puts their research and images.
**Comments and replies** left in a document for others to read later.
**Online workspaces** such as a Google Classroom stream or a shared Slides file that the group adds to over a week.
**Email**: you send it now and it is read later.

head: Synchronous
Asynchronous
rows: Each person when it suits them
Shared folders, comments, online workspaces, email
Flexible: fits round clubs, sport and homework
Hard to find a time everyone is free
Waiting for replies can slow things down

blocks.title: Worked example: synchronous or asynchronous?
blocks.context: Classify each one. (a) Grace and Callum both type in the same Doc during an ICT lesson. (b) Oisín leaves a comment on Sunday; Erin replies on Monday. (c) The group meets on a video call to plan. (d) Everyone drops their photos into a shared Drive folder during the week.
steps: (a) Same Doc, same time: **synchronous** (live co-editing).
(b) Different days: **asynchronous** (comments).
(c) Real-time conversation: **synchronous** (video call).
(d) Each person adds when they can: **asynchronous** (shared folder).
blocks.answer: (a) and (c) are synchronous; (b) and (d) are asynchronous.

blocks.text: Working on a shared document responsibly

items: **Agree who does what** before you start, e.g. one slide or section each.
**Stay in your own section.** Do not change someone else's part without asking: use a comment or suggestion instead.
**Never delete other people's work.** Version history shows exactly who did it, and your teacher can see it.
**Do your share on time**, so others are not left waiting.
**Keep comments polite and helpful.**

blocks.text: If someone deletes or spoils your group's work, do not get into an argument in the comments. Restore it with **version history** and tell your teacher.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Synchronous = at the same time: live co-editing, video calls.
Asynchronous = at different times: shared folders, comments, online workspaces, email.
Synchronous is fast but needs everyone free; asynchronous is flexible but slower.
Agree roles, stay in your section and never delete others' work.

check.q: Which is an example of synchronous collaboration?
o: Three pupils typing in the same Google Doc at the same time
Leaving a comment that a friend answers the next day
Putting photos into a shared Drive folder over a week
Sending an email that is read on Monday
check.why: Synchronous means at the same time, like live co-editing.

check.q: What does asynchronous collaboration mean?
o: People work together in the same room only
Only one person is allowed to edit the file
People work together at different times
People work together by video call
check.why: Asynchronous means not at the same time.

check.q: Which is a disadvantage of synchronous collaboration?
o: You have to wait days for any reply
It cannot be done over the internet
It can be hard to find a time when everyone is free
Nobody can see what the others are doing
check.why: Everyone needs to be online at the same time.

check.q: A group member wants to change your section. What is the responsible way?
o: Delete your section and rewrite it
Copy your section into their own file
Add a comment or suggestion for you to decide
Change the file to Viewer so you cannot edit
check.why: Comments and suggestions keep the owner of the section in control.

practice.q: Explain the difference between **synchronous** and **asynchronous** collaboration, giving an example of each.
practice.a: Synchronous: working together at the same time / in real time (1), e.g. live co-editing a Doc / a video call (1). Asynchronous: working together at different times (1), e.g. a shared folder / comments / online workspace / email (1).

practice.q: Give **one** advantage of asynchronous collaboration for a group project.
practice.a: People can contribute when it suits them / fits around other commitments / no need to find a time when all are free (1).

practice.q: State **two** rules for working responsibly on a shared document.
practice.a: Any two: agree who does what (1); stay in your own section (1); do not delete others' work (1); use comments/suggestions to propose changes (1); do your share on time (1); keep comments polite (1).

pages.spec: Upload files to Drive and Classroom, recognise common file types and convert between them
pages.summary: You can upload photos, PDFs and Word files to Drive or attach them to an assignment with Add or create. The file extension tells you the type. Google can open Word files, and can download your work as a PDF or Word document when you need a different format.

diagram.title: How long will my upload take?
diagram.caption: Change the file size (MB) and the upload speed (Mbps). Home upload speeds are often much slower than download speeds.

blocks.text: Not all your work starts life in Google Docs. You might take a photo of a model you built, scan a drawing, or make something in Microsoft Word at home. To hand it in, you **upload** it: copy it from your device up to the cloud.
Common file types
Remember the **file extension**, the letters after the dot, tells you what type of file it is.

head: Extension
Type of file
Notes
rows: Google Docs can open and edit it
Looks the same on every device; hard to edit, so good for finished work
Images, e.g. a phone photo or a screenshot
JPG is good for photos; PNG for screenshots and diagrams
Large files: they take longer to upload
blocks.caption: File types you will meet

blocks.text: Uploading

items: **To Drive**: click **New > File upload**, choose the file and click Open. You can also drag a file from your computer straight into the Drive window.
**To an assignment**: open it, click **Add or create**, then choose **File** to upload from your device, or **Google Drive** for a file already in your Drive. Then **Turn in**.
**On a phone**: the Classroom app lets you attach a photo or take one with the camera.

blocks.text: Converting files
**Converting** a file means changing it from one file type to another.

head: You want to...
Do this
rows: Edit a Word file in Google Docs
Open it from Drive; to turn it into a proper Google Doc, choose **File > Save as Google Docs**
Hand in a finished copy that cannot be changed
In Google Docs choose **File > Download > PDF document (.pdf)**
Give a file to someone who uses Microsoft Word
blocks.caption: Converting between formats

blocks.title: Worked example: how long to upload?
blocks.context: Callum filmed a 200 MB video of his rugby skills for PE. His home upload speed is 8 Mbps (megabits per second).
steps: File sizes are in **megabytes**, speeds in **megabits**. There are 8 bits in a byte.
200 MB x 8 = **1600 megabits**.
1600 / 8 Mbps = **200 seconds**.
200 seconds is about **3 minutes 20 seconds**.
blocks.answer: About 3 minutes 20 seconds, so he should not close the page until the upload has finished.

blocks.text: A file that is still uploading is **not attached** yet. If you click Turn in or close the tab too early, your teacher may get nothing. Wait until the file appears in the assignment.
If an assignment says to hand in a **PDF**, download your Doc as a PDF first, then upload the PDF. Check you have uploaded the right file by opening it before you turn in.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Upload = copy a file from your device to the cloud.
Drive: New > File upload. Assignment: Add or create > File.
.docx Word, .pptx PowerPoint, .xlsx Excel, .pdf PDF, .jpg/.png images.
Convert with File > Save as Google Docs, or File > Download as PDF or Word.
Upload time = size in MB x 8 / speed in Mbps.

check.q: Which file type is best for handing in a finished copy that looks the same on every device?
check.why: PDFs look the same everywhere and are hard to change.

check.q: How do you attach a photo from your laptop to a Classroom assignment?
check.why: Add or create > File uploads from your device.

check.q: A 40 MB file is uploaded at 8 Mbps. How long does it take?
check.why: 40 x 8 = 320 megabits; 320 / 8 = 40 seconds.

check.q: What does the extension .xlsx tell you?
o: It is a Microsoft Word document
It is a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet
check.why: .xlsx is an Excel spreadsheet.

practice.q: Describe how to download a Google Doc as a PDF.
practice.a: Open the Doc and choose File > Download (1), then choose PDF document (.pdf) (1).

practice.q: Give **one** reason a teacher might ask for work to be handed in as a PDF.
practice.a: It looks the same on any device / cannot easily be changed after handing in / keeps the layout (1).

practice.q: A 300 MB video is uploaded on a 12 Mbps connection. Calculate the upload time. Show your working.
practice.a: 300 x 8 = 2400 megabits (1); 2400 / 12 (1) = 200 seconds (about 3 minutes 20 seconds) (1).

pages.spec: Use the To-do list, calendar and notifications to stay organised and meet deadlines
pages.summary: Classroom's To-do list shows Assigned, Missing and Done work from all your classes, and the calendar shows due dates. Notifications tell you about new work. Plan backwards from the due date and start early.

diagram.title: Planning a homework due on Friday
diagram.caption: Niamh gets a homework on Monday. Click each day to see her plan.

items.label: Monday: set
items.detail: Reads the instructions and due date straight away and opens her copy. Asks a question in a private comment.

items.label: Tuesday: start
items.detail: Does the first half after school. It autosaves to Drive.

items.label: Wednesday: hockey
items.detail: No time tonight, and she planned for that.

items.label: Thursday: finish and check
items.detail: Finishes, checks spelling and reads the instructions again. Clicks Turn in.

items.label: Friday: due
items.detail: Nothing to panic about. If the Wi-Fi had gone down last night, she would still have been fine.

blocks.text: In Year 8 you will have homework from lots of subjects, with different due dates. Google Classroom has tools to help you keep track, but **you** still have to use them.
The To-do list
Click the menu (three lines, top left) and choose **To-do**. The **[[To-do list]]** gathers work from **all** your classes in one place, split into three tabs:

head: Tab
What it shows
rows: Work you still have to do, with the soonest due date first
Work that is past its due date and has not been turned in
Work you have turned in or marked as done (and work that has been returned)
blocks.caption: The To-do list

blocks.text: If something stays in **Assigned** or **Missing** even though you did it, you probably forgot to click **Turn in**.
The calendar
The **Calendar** page in Classroom shows each week with your work placed on its due date. It is a good way to see busy weeks coming. Due dates also appear in Google Calendar.
Notifications

A **notification** is an alert telling you something has happened: new work has been set, a teacher has replied to your comment, or work has been returned. Notifications come by email and, if you use the app, to your phone or tablet.
Too many notifications? Change them in Classroom's **Settings** rather than ignoring them all. Just keep the important ones on, like new work and returned work.
Managing deadlines

items: **Check Classroom every day**, at the same time, e.g. when you get home.
**Read the due date and time** carefully. Some work is due at a set time, like 9:00 on Monday.
**Plan backwards** from the due date: when will you start, and when will you finish?
**Start early**: the internet going down the night before is not a good excuse.
**Do not leave turning in till the last minute**: you may hit an upload problem.
**If you are stuck or off sick**, send your teacher a private comment *before* the deadline.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Jack do first?
blocks.context: It is Tuesday evening. Jack's To-do list shows: Science worksheet (due Wednesday), History poster (due next Monday), ICT quiz (due Friday) and, under Missing, a Maths homework from last week.
steps: The **Missing** Maths homework is already late: do it tonight and add a private comment explaining.
The **Science** worksheet is due tomorrow: do it tonight too.
The **ICT** quiz (Friday) can be done on Wednesday or Thursday.
The **History** poster (Monday) is a bigger task: plan to start it on Thursday and finish at the weekend.
blocks.answer: Missing work and tomorrow's work first, then plan the rest by due date.

blocks.title: Key points
items: To-do list: Assigned, Missing and Done, from all classes.
Calendar: work shown on its due date.
Notifications: alerts by email or app about new and returned work.
Check daily, plan backwards from the due date and start early.
Missing usually means not turned in.

check.q: Which To-do tab shows work that is past its due date and has not been turned in?
check.why: Missing = past the due date and not turned in.

check.q: Grace did her homework but it still shows under Assigned. What is the most likely reason?
o: The To-do list only updates once a week
check.why: Work stays in Assigned until it is turned in.

check.q: What is a notification?
o: A comment that only your teacher can see
An alert telling you something has happened, like new work being set
A file shared with commenter permission
A copy of a file kept in the Bin
check.why: Notifications alert you to new work, replies and returned work.

check.q: What is the best way to plan a homework that is due in a week?
o: Plan backwards from the due date and start early
Wait for a reminder the night before
Turn it in empty and finish it later
check.why: Planning backwards and starting early leaves time for problems.

practice.q: Name the **three** tabs of the Google Classroom To-do list and state what each shows.
practice.a: Assigned: work still to do (1); Missing: past the due date and not turned in (1); Done: work turned in/marked as done (1).

practice.q: Give **two** ways a pupil can avoid missing a deadline.
practice.a: Any two: check Classroom/To-do daily (1); use the calendar (1); keep notifications on (1); plan backwards / start early (1); turn in before the last minute (1).

practice.q: Explain why it is unwise to leave turning in your work until ten minutes before the deadline.
practice.a: Something could go wrong, e.g. internet failure / upload problem / wrong account (1), and the work would then be late or missing (1).

pages.spec: Communicate appropriately for your audience, and act as a responsible digital citizen: avoiding plagiarism, protecting personal data and keeping your account secure
pages.summary: Match how you write to your audience: polite and clear to a teacher, friendly but kind to a friend. Never copy other people's work as your own, credit your sources, keep personal data out of shared documents, never share your password and always log out of shared computers.

diagram.title: What should you do?
diagram.caption: Match each situation to the responsible action.
pairs: You found a great paragraph online for your project
Put it in your own words and say where it came from
A friend asks for your password to hand in your work for you
Say no: never share your password
You are leaving a school computer
Sign out of Google and log off
A group Doc has a list of everyone's home addresses
Remove it: that is personal data
You need to ask your teacher for more time
Send a polite private comment
A classmate posts a mean class comment
Do not reply; tell your teacher

blocks.text: **[[Digital citizenship]]** means using technology safely, responsibly and respectfully. Google Classroom is a school space, so the same standards apply as in the classroom, even when you are at home in your pyjamas.
Writing for your audience
Digital communication follows **[[protocols|Communication protocol]]**: agreed rules for how to communicate. The right protocol depends on your **audience**: who you are writing to.

head: Writing to a teacher
Writing to a friend
rows: Full sentences, proper spelling and punctuation
Polite and to the point; say what you need
Friendly, but remember it can be screenshotted

blocks.title: Worked example: improve this private comment
blocks.context: Oisín writes to his teacher: "wat r we meant 2 do?? i wasnt here lol"
steps: Use a greeting and full words.
Say clearly what the problem is and why.
Ask a clear question.
Say thank you and sign off with your name.
blocks.answer: "Hello Mr Butler, I was absent on Tuesday and I am not sure what to do for this homework. Should I complete the worksheet attached? Thank you, Oisín."

blocks.text: Class comments: be kind

items: Only post comments that are about the work and help the class.
Never post anything rude, mean or embarrassing about anyone. Teachers can see every comment, and comments can be reported.
Remember your **digital footprint**: what you write online can be saved and shared.

blocks.text: Plagiarism and copyright

**[[Plagiarism]]** is copying someone else's work, words or ideas and passing them off as your own. It includes copying from a website, from a friend, or getting an AI chatbot to write your work for you when your teacher has not allowed it. Version history shows teachers when a large chunk of text is pasted in at once.

The person who creates a piece of work automatically owns the **copyright** to it. You can usually use small parts of other people's work in schoolwork, but you must **put it in your own words** and **credit your sources** (say where it came from, e.g. the website name and address).
Personal data and the law

**[[Personal data]]** is any information about a living person that could identify them: their name with their address, phone number, date of birth, photo, or even their medical notes. In the UK, the **[[UK GDPR]]** and the **Data Protection Act 2018** are laws that say personal data must be collected only when needed, kept secure and not shared without good reason.

Shared documents can spread personal data quickly. Do not put classmates' home addresses, phone numbers or private details in a shared Doc or Sheet, and never share a file that contains other people's personal data with people who do not need it.
Keeping your account secure

items: **Never share your password**, not even with your best friend. Anyone with it can read, change, delete or hand in work as you.
**Always sign out** of Google and **log off** when you leave a school or library computer.
**Do not leave a computer unlocked**: someone could post comments in your name.
If you think someone knows your password, tell your teacher and get it changed.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Write for your audience: formal and polite to teachers, friendly but kind to friends.
Plagiarism = passing off others' work as your own. Credit sources and use your own words.
Personal data is protected by UK GDPR: keep it out of shared documents.
Never share your password; always sign out of shared computers.

check.q: Which private comment is most suitable to send to a teacher?
o: wat homework?? i wasnt in lol
HELLO I NEED THE HOMEWORK NOW
hey u, send me the work
Hello Miss, I was absent on Monday. Could you tell me which worksheet to do? Thank you, Erin.
check.why: It is polite, clear and signed, which suits the audience.

check.q: What is plagiarism?
o: Sharing a file with commenter permission
Passing off someone else's work or words as your own
Uploading a PDF to Google Drive
check.why: Plagiarism means presenting others' work as yours.

check.q: Which law protects personal data in the UK?
o: UK GDPR (with the Data Protection Act 2018)
check.why: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 cover personal data.

check.q: You are leaving a computer in the school library. What should you do?
o: Leave it on so the next pupil can use your files
Close the lid of the screen only
Sign out of Google and log off
Clear the Bin in Google Drive
check.why: Signing out stops others using your account.

check.q: Which of these is personal data?
o: A classmate's home address and phone number
The title of your science homework
The number of slides in a presentation
check.why: It identifies and locates a living person.

practice.q: Explain how a message to a teacher should differ from a message to a friend.
practice.a: To a teacher: formal / polite greeting, full sentences and correct spelling, no text speak or emojis (1). To a friend: can be more relaxed/informal, but still kind (1).

practice.q: What is plagiarism and how can a pupil avoid it?
practice.a: Copying/passing off someone else's work as your own (1); put information in your own words and credit/reference the source (1).

practice.q: Explain why personal data should not be put in a shared Google Doc.
practice.a: Many people can see / re-share it (1); it could be misused and data protection law (UK GDPR) says it must be kept secure / only shared when needed (1).

pages.spec: Solve common problems with Google Classroom and Drive, such as missing assignments, failed uploads and the wrong account
pages.summary: Most problems have simple causes: the wrong account, not clicking Turn in, a poor connection or a file that is too big. Check the account first, then the obvious things, and tell your teacher before the deadline if you still cannot fix it.

diagram.title: I can't see my assignment!
diagram.caption: Click each step. Work through them in order before asking for help.

nodes.label: Can't find it
nodes.detail: The assignment is not where you expected.

nodes.label: Right account?
nodes.detail: Click your profile picture. Is it your @c2ken.net school account? If not, switch account.

nodes.label: Right class?
nodes.detail: Check the class name. Maybe it was set in your form class or a different group.

nodes.label: Look in Classwork and To-do
nodes.detail: Check every topic on Classwork, and the Assigned and Missing tabs of the To-do list.

nodes.label: Refresh
nodes.detail: Reload the page or close and reopen the app.

nodes.label: Ask your teacher
nodes.detail: Still missing? Tell your teacher before the deadline, not after.

blocks.text: Technology does not always do what you want. Good digital skills include **troubleshooting**: working out what is wrong, step by step, and fixing it yourself where you can. Here are the most common Classroom problems and what to do.

head: Problem
Likely cause
What to try
rows: Click your profile picture, switch to your @c2ken.net account
Wrong account, a typing mistake, or the code has been changed
Check the account; type the 6 to 8 characters exactly; ask your teacher
Wrong class, or it is under a topic you have not checked
Use the To-do list; check every topic on Classwork
It says Missing but I did it
Open it and click Turn in; add a private comment
Poor internet, the file is very large, or the page was closed too soon
Check the connection, wait for the upload to finish, try a smaller file or convert it to PDF
You have already turned it in, or you only have viewer permission
Unsubmit it, or ask the owner for editor access
The browser or device needs a restart
Refresh the page, close other tabs, restart the device
blocks.caption: Common problems and fixes

blocks.text: The wrong account problem

This is the most common problem by far, especially at home where a family computer may already be signed in to someone else's Google account. You can be signed in to several accounts at once, and Google may open Classroom in the wrong one.

items: Click your **profile picture** in the top right.
Check the email address: it should end in **@c2ken.net**.
If not, choose your school account from the list, or **Add another account** and sign in.
Tip: use a separate browser profile, or a private/incognito window, for school work on a shared family computer.

blocks.title: Worked example: Erin's missing homework
blocks.context: Erin is at home. She opens Classroom on the family laptop and sees only one class called 'Mum's Book Club'. Her ICT homework is due tomorrow.
steps: **Symptom**: none of her school classes are showing.
**Likely cause**: Classroom is open in her mum's personal account, not her school account.
**Fix**: click the profile picture, switch to *her username@c2ken.net*, and her classes appear.
**Afterwards**: sign out of her account when she has finished so her work stays private.
blocks.answer: It was the wrong account. Checking the account first fixes it in seconds.

blocks.text: When to ask for help

Try the simple fixes first, but do not spend all night stuck. If you still cannot hand in your work, **tell your teacher before the deadline**, using a private comment or school email. Explain what you tried. A message sent *before* the deadline shows you were organised; an excuse the next day does not.
Never ask a friend to sign in as you to fix a problem, and never use someone else's account to hand in your work. That breaks the school's Acceptable Use Policy.
A screenshot of an error message (**Windows + Shift + S** on Windows) helps your teacher or the technician see exactly what went wrong.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Check the account first: is it @c2ken.net?
Missing work usually means Turn in was not clicked.
Upload problems: connection, file size, closing the page too soon.
Lost work: check the Bin and version history.
Still stuck? Tell your teacher before the deadline, and say what you tried.

check.q: At home, Callum's classes have disappeared from Classroom. What should he check first?
o: Which account he is signed in with
The file extension of his homework
check.why: The wrong account is the most common cause.

check.q: Ruairí cannot edit his document inside an assignment he has turned in. Why?
o: Turned-in work is locked until you unsubmit or it is returned
Google Docs only allows editing in school
His teacher has deleted the file
The file has been converted to a PNG
check.why: Turned-in work cannot be edited until you unsubmit or the teacher returns it.

check.q: A large video will not upload to an assignment. Which is NOT a sensible thing to try?
o: Waiting for the upload to complete
Turning in before the upload has finished
check.why: Turning in early means the teacher gets no file.

check.q: You still cannot hand in your work the night before the deadline. What should you do?
o: Wait and explain the next week
Ask a friend to sign in as you
Send your teacher a message before the deadline explaining what you tried
check.why: Tell your teacher before the deadline, and say what you tried.

practice.q: A pupil says their Google Classroom classes have all disappeared. Describe how they could fix the most likely cause.
practice.a: Check which account is signed in by clicking the profile picture (1); switch to/add the school @c2ken.net account (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why a file might fail to upload to an assignment.
practice.a: Any two: poor/no internet connection (1); file too large (1); page closed / turned in before upload finished (1); file type not supported (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should contact your teacher **before** a deadline if you have a technical problem.
practice.a: Shows you were organised / not just making an excuse (1); the teacher can help or give more time before it is marked missing/late (1).

glossary.def: Storage, software and services on servers in data centres that you use over the internet instead of on your own device.
Saving files on a provider's servers so they can be reached over the internet from any device.
Storage that is somewhere other than the device you are using, such as cloud storage or a school server.
Saving files on the device itself (its hard drive or SSD) or on a USB stick plugged into it.
A large building full of servers that store data and run cloud services 24 hours a day.
Using software that runs on remote servers over the internet, such as Google Docs in a web browser.
The harm to the environment from using technology, e.g. the electricity, water and carbon emissions of data centres.
A website and app where teachers post work, notes and announcements, and pupils hand in their work.
A code of 6 to 8 letters and numbers that a pupil types in once to join a Google Classroom class.
The page in a Classroom class showing announcements and posts about new work.
The page in a Classroom class listing all assignments, questions and materials, grouped into topics.
A piece of work set in Google Classroom for pupils to complete and hand in.
To hand in an assignment in Google Classroom so the teacher can mark it.
To take back turned-in work so it can be changed; it must then be turned in again.
Google's cloud storage, where Google files and uploaded files are saved and organised into folders.
Where deleted Google Drive files go; they can be restored for 30 days before being permanently deleted.
The software that manages a computer's resources, peripherals, files and security, e.g. Windows.
An everyday choice that reduces the energy and storage your digital activity uses, e.g. deleting files you no longer need.
Google's online word processor for letters, essays and reports.
A feature that saves every change automatically as you work.
A record of earlier versions of a file, showing who changed what and when, which can be restored.
The level of access given to a person when a file is shared: viewer, commenter or editor.
A sharing permission that only lets someone open and read a file.
A sharing permission that lets someone read a file and add comments and suggestions, but not edit it directly.
A sharing permission that lets someone change anything in a file.
A mode in Google Docs where changes appear in colour as suggestions for the owner to accept or reject.
Working together at the same time, in real time, e.g. live co-editing or a video call.
Working together at different times, e.g. shared folders, comments, online workspaces or email.
Portable Document Format: a file type that looks the same on every device and is hard to edit.
The Google Classroom page that gathers work from all classes into Assigned, Missing and Done.
Using technology safely, responsibly and respectfully.
Agreed rules for how to communicate, chosen to suit the audience, such as how formally to write to a teacher.
Copying someone else's work, words or ideas and passing them off as your own.
Any information about a living person that could identify them, such as name with address, phone number or photo.
The UK law (with the Data Protection Act 2018) that controls how personal data is collected, stored and shared.
